content_html:
The internal rate of return (IRR) is the single yearly rate that sums up how well an investment pays you back, taking into account both how much you get and when you get it. It is the discount rate at which the money you put in and the money you take out balance exactly in today's dollars. This calculator finds that rate for any series of cash flows and also shows the net present value (NPV) at a discount rate you choose, the payback period and a period-by-period breakdown.

How to use this calculator

  1. Initial investment: what you pay at the start, such as the price of equipment, a property down payment or the cost of a business project.
  2. Cash flow period: whether each row below is a year, half-year, quarter or month. The IRR is always reported as an annual rate so different projects can be compared.
  3. Discount rate for NPV: the yearly return you could reasonably earn elsewhere, or the return you require before taking on the investment.
  4. Cash flow each period: money you receive is positive. If you have to put more money in later, enter it as a negative number. Use Add period for longer projects (up to 60 periods) and include any sale or final payout in the last period.

How IRR is calculated

Each future cash flow is discounted back to today by dividing it by (1 + r)t, where t is the number of periods until it arrives. Adding up all the discounted amounts, including the negative initial investment, gives the net present value:

NPV = CF0 + CF1 ÷ (1 + r) + CF2 ÷ (1 + r)2 + … + CFn ÷ (1 + r)n

The IRR is the rate r that makes this sum exactly zero. There is no direct formula for it, so the calculator searches for it numerically to a fraction of a basis point. When the periods are shorter than a year, the per-period rate is converted to an annual rate with (1 + r)k − 1, where k is the number of periods in a year.

A worked example

Suppose a project costs $10,000 and returns $2,000, $3,000, $4,000, $4,000 and $3,000 over the next five years. In total you get back $16,000, a net gain of $6,000 and a money multiple of 1.60×. The IRR is 16.60% a year: discounting every payment at 16.60% brings their combined value back to exactly $10,000.

At an 8% discount rate the same cash flows have an NPV of $2,581.07, meaning the project is worth about $2,581 more in today's money than an investment earning 8%. The cumulative cash turns positive a quarter of the way through year 4, so the payback period is 3.25 years.

Reading the results

  • IRR above your discount rate and a positive NPV both suggest the investment beats your alternative. If they disagree when you compare two projects, NPV is usually the better guide because it measures the gain in dollars.
  • Payback period ignores what happens after you recover your money, so a project can pay back quickly yet earn a low IRR.
  • Several IRRs: when cash flows switch between positive and negative more than once, more than one rate can make NPV zero. The calculator lists every rate it finds and shows the one closest to your discount rate.

Tips for better estimates

  • Use after-tax cash flows if you are comparing with an after-tax alternative, and include ongoing costs such as maintenance or fees.
  • IRR assumes interim cash can be reinvested at the IRR itself. For very high IRRs that is optimistic, so treat them as an upper bound.
  • Try a cautious and an optimistic set of cash flows to see how sensitive the result is to your assumptions.

faq.question: What is a good IRR?
faq.answer: It depends on the risk and on what else you could do with the money. An IRR is attractive when it is comfortably above your cost of capital or the return you could earn on a comparable investment, often called the hurdle rate.

faq.question: What is the difference between IRR and ROI?
faq.answer: ROI compares total profit with the amount invested and ignores timing. IRR accounts for when each dollar arrives, so a project that pays back sooner has a higher IRR than one with the same total profit spread over more years.

faq.question: Why does the calculator say the IRR is not defined?
faq.answer: An IRR only exists when the cash flows include at least one outflow and one inflow and some rate makes their net present value zero. If every cash flow is positive or every one is negative, no such rate exists.

faq.question: How does this IRR compare with the Excel IRR function?
faq.answer: For evenly spaced yearly cash flows the results match Excel's IRR function. For quarterly or monthly cash flows this calculator also annualizes the result, so it equals (1 + Excel IRR) raised to the number of periods per year, minus 1.

faq.question: Can I use this for cash flows on irregular dates?
faq.answer: This calculator assumes equally spaced periods. For payments on irregular dates you need a date-based method such as XIRR, or you can approximate by using monthly periods and entering zero for months with no cash flow.
